sections.preamble: You are an expert coding assistant operating inside pi, a coding agent harness. You help users by reading files, executing commands, editing code, and writing new files.
sections.tools:
<tools>
- read: Read file contents
- bash: Execute bash commands (ls, grep, find, etc.)
- edit: Make precise file edits with exact text replacement, including multiple disjoint edits in one call
- write: Create or overwrite files

In addition to the tools above, you may have access to other custom tools depending on the project.
</tools>
sections.rules:
<rules>
- Use bash for file operations like ls, rg, find
- Use read to examine files instead of cat or sed.
- You can inspect PI_* environment variables for current model and session details.
- Use edit for precise changes (edits[].oldText must match exactly)
- When changing multiple separate locations in one file, use one edit call with multiple entries in edits[] instead of multiple edit calls
- Each edits[].oldText is matched against the original file, not after earlier edits are applied. Do not emit overlapping or nested edits. Merge nearby changes into one edit.
- Keep edits[].oldText as small as possible while still being unique in the file. Do not pad with large unchanged regions.
- Use write only for new files or complete rewrites.
- Be concise in your responses
- Show file paths clearly when working with files
</rules>

content.text:
Create an animated, non-interactive surfing pelican using html/3js

Build this as an interactive web page in the current directory.
- The entry point is index.html. Put your code in JavaScript ES modules loaded from it
  (`<script type="module" src="main.js">`), and add a short README.md.
- You may use npm packages: `npm install <package>` here, then import them by name
  (`import * as THREE from "three"`). No CDN URLs and no import maps.
- Afterwards the page is packaged into one self-contained index.html with esbuild: every script and
  stylesheet index.html references is bundled with everything it imports. Load assets the page needs
  with `import` (they become data URLs) or generate them in code, never by URL string.
- The packaged page runs offline in a sandboxed iframe: no network requests, and no localStorage,
  cookies or other storage (they throw there).
- Check that it packages: `esbuild main.js --bundle --format=esm --outfile=/dev/null` must succeed.
  Don't build or package the page yourself; that happens afterwards.
- Only create or edit files inside the current directory.
- Finish with a short summary of what you built.

# Surfing Pelican

An animated, non-interactive three.js scene: a pelican rides a surfboard across an
endless Gerstner-wave ocean under a warm afternoon sun, with spray, foam, circling
gulls and a slow drifting camera. No input required — just watch.

## Run

```bash
npm install
# any static server works, e.g.
npx serve .
# or open index.html through a local server of your choice
```

Then open `index.html` in a browser.

## Package

```bash
esbuild main.js --bundle --format=esm --outfile=bundle.js
```

Everything is generated in code (procedural geometry + canvas textures), so the
bundled page is fully self-contained and works offline.

## Files

| File        | Purpose                                                                    |
| ----------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `index.html`| Page shell, inline styles, loads `main.js` as an ES module                 |
| `main.js`   | Scene setup, lights, camera orbit, animation loop, surfer placement        |
| `waves.js`  | Shared Gerstner wave field — generates both the GLSL and the JS sampler    |
| `ocean.js`  | Sky dome, sun glow, wave-shaded ocean, spray particles, contact shadow     |
| `pelican.js`| Procedural pelican (body, swept neck, beak + pouch, wings, feet) and board |
| `birds.js`  | Distant flock of gulls circling on the horizon                             |

## Notes

- The ocean surface is displaced in the vertex shader from the wave list in
  `waves.js`; the same list is evaluated in JavaScript every frame so the
  pelican, board, spray and contact shadow ride the exact same water surface,
  including its slope.
- Shading is hand written GLSL (depth tint, fresnel sky reflection, sun glints,
  crest foam broken up with value noise) and uses three.js' fog chunks so the
  ocean dissolves into the sky at the horizon.
- The pelican is entirely procedural geometry: lathed/tapered boxes, a tube swept
  along a Catmull-Rom curve for the neck, and extruded bezier shapes for the
  wings, feathers and fin.

## Summary

**Surfing Pelican** — an animated, non-interactive three.js scene in `index.html` + ES modules, built entirely from procedural geometry and canvas-generated textures (no URLs, no storage, fully offline-capable).

**Files**
- `index.html` — page shell with inline styles (vignette + caption), loads `main.js` as a module
- `main.js` — renderer/scene/lights, slow orbiting camera that keeps the surfer framed, animation loop, and per-frame placement of the surfer on the water
- `waves.js` — one Gerstner wave list that generates **both** the GLSL vertex displacement and the JavaScript sampler, so the pelican, board, spray and shadow ride the exact same water surface and slope
- `ocean.js` — gradient sky dome with sun bloom, hand-written water shader (depth tint, fresnel sky reflection, sun glints, noise-broken crest foam with distance-faded detail to avoid far-field aliasing), soft spray particles and a contact shadow that follows the wave normal
- `pelican.js` — procedural bird: ellipsoid body, neck swept along a Catmull-Rom curve as a variable-radius tube, tapered/hooked beak with a breathing gular pouch, extruded-bezier wings with layered feathers and black primaries (mirrored left wing, flapping with phase lag), webbed feet, and a vertex-color painted surfboard with fin
- `birds.js` — seven distant gulls circling the horizon
- `README.md`, `package.json` (`three` is the only dependency)

**Verified**: `esbuild main.js --bundle --format=esm --outfile=/dev/null` succeeds, and I rendered the page in headless Chromium — no console errors or NaN geometry warnings, and the framing/animation look right at several points in the orbit.
